Adult Soffie (Parachondrostoma toxostoma) typically attain a total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], representing the maximum size recorded for this cyprinid species in its native Rhône basin. This asymptotic dimension is accompanied by a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 319 grams [Wwi = 319 grams], a mass consistent with the slender, fusiform body plan characteristic of rheophilic fishes adapted to fast-flowing Mediterranean rivers. Field surveys conducted over multiple seasons indicate that females reach sexual maturity at a significantly smaller length, with puberty estimated to occur at a total length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters]. The body mass associated with this developmental milestone is approximately 18.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 18.5 grams], reflecting the substantial energetic investment required to transition from a juvenile, somatic-growth-dominated phase to one capable of supporting gonadal development and eventual spawning. These length-weight relationships, derived from extensive specimen series, align well with the general morphometric patterns observed across the genus Parachondrostoma.

Neonatal body mass in Soffie is remarkably low, with newly emerged larvae weighing just 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 1.7 millimeters and the spherical volume formula. This minimal initial mass places the species toward the lower end of the range reported for other cyprinids of comparable adult size. The tiny yolk-sac larvae are entirely dependent on endogenous reserves during the first days post-hatching, a period of rapid morphogenesis during which the mouth and digestive tract develop sufficiently to allow first exogenous feeding. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the transition from yolk absorption to active feeding occurs within a matter of days, a schedule that accelerates considerably relative to cooler regimes. The combination of a very small hatchling mass and a relatively warm developmental environment suggests that Soffie follows a strategy of early rapid growth to escape the high predation pressures characteristic of its gravel-bed spawning habitats.

Reproductive output in Soffie has been quantified through controlled spawning experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females were observed to produce approximately 41 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 41 eggs per spawning event], with individual females completing an average of one spawning event each year [F_R_i = one spawning event each year]. This reproductive schedule, combining a moderate clutch size with an annual spawning frequency, is broadly consistent with the iteroparous life-history strategy seen in other Mediterranean cyprinids inhabiting unpredictable, flow-variable environments. The relatively low fecundity per event compared to some potamodromous cyprinids may reflect a trade-off favoring larger egg size—the 1.7 millimeter diameter ensures sufficient yolk reserves for the larva to reach the critical first-feeding stage—rather than maximizing numerical output. Field observations corroborate that spawning typically coincides with spring high-flow events.

Longevity data for Soffie, derived from mark-recapture studies and scale-reading analyses conducted in populations maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days], equivalent to roughly eight years. This lifespan is moderate for a cyprinid of its body size, falling within the range reported for other rheophilic species such as the common nase (Chondrostoma nasus), which can live slightly longer, but notably shorter than the decades-long lifespans observed in larger, potamodromous cyprinids. The relatively compressed life cycle, combined with early maturation at 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters] total length, suggests a life-history strategy geared toward ensuring at least several reproductive seasons before senescence and natural death occur. Age-at-death distributions from field collections show that mortality increases sharply after the sixth year, with very few individuals surviving to the maximum recorded eight-year mark.

A comparative perspective reveals that the body morphology of Soffie is strongly shaped by its lotic environment. The ultimate total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] and the corresponding wet weight at puberty of 18.5 grams [Wwp = 18.5 grams] position this species as a medium-sized member of its genus, with a more elongate body form than the deeper-bodied, lentic-adapted species. The wet weight at birth of 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams] is particularly instructive when compared to that of congeneric species spawning in cooler, more stable headwaters; those species tend to produce slightly larger, more yolk-rich eggs, suggesting that the thermal regime experienced by Soffie at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] influences both egg size and the subsequent rapid growth necessary for juvenile survival. The maximum recorded reproductive rate, expressed as approximately 41 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 41 eggs per spawning event] occurring once per year [F_R_i = once per year], underscores a strategy of moderate, annual reproductive investment that matches the productivity of its Mediterranean river habitat.
